title: HTML Elements: what, when and why
intro: A quiz about HTML elements — what each one does, when to use it and when not, its effect on accessibility (implicit ARIA role), and its Baseline status. Learn from positive and negative examples with feedback on every answer. For HTML learners, beginner to advanced. Status facts are as of October 2025.

questions.text: A page wraps its main article in <div class="content">. Which element best marks the page's main content?

options.info: <main> marks the page's dominant content and carries the implicit role "main". A page has exactly one <main>, and screen readers offer it as a landmark to jump to.
A <div> is a generic container with no semantic role, so the id "main" adds no meaning for assistive technology. The region is not announced as a landmark.
<section> marks a thematic section and needs its own heading. It does not mean "the main content of the page".
<article> marks a self-contained, independently distributable piece such as a blog post. It is not the wrapper for all of a page's main content.

questions.explanation: <main> is the one element for a page's primary content; it gives a "main" landmark for free, which a <div> never does.

questions.text: You have a list of links to the site's primary pages. Which element marks it as navigation?

options.info: <nav> marks a block of major navigation links and gives the implicit role "navigation", which screen readers expose as a landmark.
A class name styles the box but gives it no role; assistive technology sees a plain container, not navigation.
<menu> is a semantic list of commands/items (a variant of <ul>); it is not the landmark for site navigation.
<aside> marks content tangential to the main content, such as a sidebar note; its role is "complementary", not navigation.

questions.explanation: <nav> names a navigation landmark. Not every group of links needs <nav> — reserve it for major blocks like the primary menu.

questions.text: Wrapping every part of a layout in <div> elements gives assistive technology the same structure as using <header>, <nav>, <main> and <footer>.
questions.explanation: A <div> carries no role, so a layout built only from <div> offers no landmarks. Semantic sectioning elements let screen-reader users jump straight to the header, navigation, main content or footer.

questions.text: Which element marks introductory content — a logo, site title and intro — at the top of the page?

options.info: <header> groups introductory content or navigational aids. At the top level of the page it exposes a "banner" landmark.
<head> holds metadata (title, meta, links to CSS) and is never rendered in the page body. It is not a visible header region.
There is no <top> element in HTML.
A styled <div> looks like a header but has no role, so it is not announced as the banner landmark.

questions.explanation: <header> is the sectioning element for introductory content; at page level it is the banner landmark. <head> is metadata, a different thing entirely.

questions.text: Which element marks the page's closing region with copyright and contact details?

options.info: <footer> holds closing content for its nearest section; at page level it exposes the "contentinfo" landmark.
There is no <bottom> element in HTML.
<aside> is for tangential content, not for a page's closing footer.
<section> is a generic thematic section; it does not expose the contentinfo landmark that <footer> gives at page level.

questions.explanation: <footer> marks closing content and, at page level, the contentinfo landmark — a <section> would not.

questions.text: A blog post could be syndicated to a feed reader on its own. Which element marks it best?

options.info: <article> marks a self-contained composition that could stand alone or be distributed independently, like a blog post, a news item or a comment.
<section> groups related content inside a document but does not imply it is independently distributable.
<div> is a generic container and says nothing about the content being self-contained.
<main> is the single primary-content region of the whole page, not the marker for one independently distributable post.

questions.explanation: The test for <article> is independence: if the piece makes sense on its own and could be syndicated, <article> fits.

questions.text: <section> is the right default container to use whenever you just need to group elements for styling.
questions.explanation: For a purely stylistic group with no thematic meaning, use <div>. <section> is for a thematic grouping, normally with its own heading; using it as a styling box clutters the outline with empty regions.

questions.text: A <section> should contain a heading so it has an accessible label in the document outline.
questions.explanation: Each <section> normally starts with a heading (<h1>–<h6>). Without one, the region has no accessible name, so it is hard to identify in an outline or a list of landmarks.

questions.text: What is the common, recommended convention for the top-level heading of a page?

options.text: One <h1> that names the whole page
options.info: A single <h1> gives the page one clear title at the top of the heading hierarchy, which helps users scan the outline. It is a widely recommended convention.

options.text: An <h1> at the start of every paragraph
options.info: Headings are not paragraph markers; an <h1> per paragraph destroys the outline and overwhelms screen-reader navigation.

options.text: No heading at all, styled text instead
options.info: Visually styled text that is not a heading gives no structure to assistive technology; the page then has no navigable outline.

options.text: Several <h1> elements, one per colour theme
options.info: Headings describe structure, not styling. Reusing <h1> for themes is not what heading levels mean.

questions.explanation: A single, descriptive <h1> at the top is the clear, conventional choice; heading levels build the outline, they are not styling hooks.

questions.text: Jumping from <h2> straight to <h4> and skipping <h3> can confuse the document outline for screen-reader users.
questions.explanation: Heading levels should not skip: go h2 then h3, not h2 then h4. Screen-reader users rely on the levels to understand nesting, and a skipped level suggests a missing section.

questions.text: You need text that looks big and bold but is not a section title. What should you do?

options.text: Use a normal element and style it with CSS
options.info: Appearance is CSS's job. A heading element must mean "this starts a section", so text that only needs to look large should be styled, not marked up as a heading.

options.text: Use <h1> because it is the biggest by default
options.info: Choosing a heading for its default size misuses the outline; <h1> means "page title", not "large text".
<big> is a deprecated, obsolete element removed from the standard; use CSS font-size instead.
<font> is a deprecated, obsolete presentational element; styling belongs in CSS.

questions.explanation: Pick a heading for meaning, not size. For purely visual emphasis, use CSS — never a deprecated presentational element.

questions.text: You have an image with a caption that explains it. Which combination marks this correctly?

options.info: <figure> groups self-contained content such as an image, and <figcaption> gives it a caption that is programmatically associated with the figure.

options.text:
followed by a

with the caption text
options.info: A following paragraph is not linked to the image, so assistive technology does not know the paragraph is its caption.
Generic containers do not associate the caption with the image; there is no figure/figcaption relationship.
<picture> provides responsive image sources and has no caption slot; <legend> belongs to <fieldset>, not to images.

questions.explanation: <figure> + <figcaption> is the pair for captioned, self-contained content; the caption is tied to the figure, unlike a stray paragraph.

questions.text: A <figcaption> must be the first or last child of its <figure>.
questions.explanation: <figcaption> represents a caption for its parent <figure> and, per the HTML spec, must be the figure's first or last child. In between it would not be a valid caption.

questions.text: Which kinds of content can a <figure> sensibly wrap? Select every correct answer.

options.info: Images are the classic figure content, with <figcaption> as the caption.
A <figure> can group a code block (for example a <pre>) with a caption describing it.
A <figure> may wrap a <blockquote> with a <figcaption> that attributes or explains it.
Navigation is not self-contained referenced content; it belongs in <nav>, not in a <figure>.

questions.explanation: <figure> is for self-contained content referenced from the main flow — images, code, diagrams, quotations — not for site navigation.

questions.text: Which element gives a data table a title that screen readers announce with the table?

options.info: <caption> is the table's title and must be the first child of <table>; assistive technology announces it when the user enters the table.
A paragraph before the table is not associated with it, so it is not announced as the table's caption.
<title> sets the document title in the browser tab; it has nothing to do with a table's caption.
A heading in a cell is content of that cell, not a caption for the whole table.

questions.explanation: <caption>, placed as the first child of <table>, is the accessible, announced title of a table.

questions.text: In a data table, how should the cells that label each column be marked?

options.info: <th> marks a header cell, and scope="col" says it heads its column, so each data cell is linked to its column header for screen-reader users.
A styled <td> is still a data cell with no header semantics; assistive technology does not treat it as a header.
<thead> groups header rows but the cells themselves must still be <th> to be header cells; <td> inside is just data.
<label> is for form controls, not table columns.

questions.explanation: Header cells are <th>, and scope (col or row) ties data cells to their headers — essential for understanding a table without sight.

questions.text: Using a <table> purely to position boxes side by side for layout is the recommended modern approach.
questions.explanation: Tables are for tabular data. For layout, use CSS (flexbox or grid). A layout table confuses assistive technology, which announces rows, columns and headers that carry no meaning.

questions.text: Match each sectioning element to the region it marks.

pairs.right: Content tangential to the main content

questions.explanation: Each sectioning element names a region: navigation, main content, complementary aside and closing footer. Choosing them over <div> gives screen-reader users landmarks.

questions.text: A sidebar holds related links and a pull quote, separate from the article's argument. Which element fits?

options.info: <aside> marks content tangentially related to the content around it, such as a sidebar; its implicit role is "complementary".
<section> is a thematic part of the main flow, not specifically tangential/complementary content.
<div> would work as a box but gives no "complementary" landmark.
<footer> is for closing content of a section or page, not a sidebar of related extras.

questions.explanation: <aside> is for content that is related but separate — a sidebar or pull quote — and exposes the complementary landmark.

questions.text: An <article> may contain its own <section> elements to divide its content into parts.
questions.explanation: Sectioning elements nest: an <article> can hold several <section> parts (for example "Introduction", "Method"), each with its own heading. The relationship is about meaning, not a fixed order.

questions.text: You want a title with a subtitle directly under it, treated as one heading. Which element groups them?

options.text: <hgroup> around the <h1> and the subtitle paragraph
options.info: <hgroup> groups a heading with secondary content such as a tagline or subtitle, so they read as a single heading block.
Two <h1> elements create two top-level headings, which breaks the single-title convention and the outline.

options.text: An <h1> and an <h2> for the subtitle
options.info: An <h2> subtitle starts a new, lower-level section rather than acting as a subtitle of the same heading; <hgroup> is the element made for this.
Re-creating a heading with ARIA on a <div> is worse than using native heading markup; it needs aria-level and loses built-in behaviour.

questions.explanation: <hgroup> is the purpose-built wrapper for a heading plus its subtitle/tagline, keeping one heading in the outline.

questions.text: A <header> placed inside an <article> still exposes the page-level banner landmark.
questions.explanation: A <header> is the banner landmark only when it is a top-level header of the page. Inside an <article> or <section> it is just that section's introductory header, with no banner role.

questions.text: You have terms each followed by their definition (a glossary). Which element pairs them semantically?

options.info: A description list <dl> associates each term <dt> with one or more descriptions <dd>, which is exactly a glossary or name/value set.

options.text: <ul> with <li> for both term and definition
options.info: An unordered list has no term/description relationship; it is just a flat list of items.
A table implies a grid of data; a term/description pairing is better expressed as a description list.
An ordered list numbers items; a glossary is name/value pairs, not a ranked sequence.

questions.explanation: <dl>/<dt>/<dd> is the semantic structure for term-and-description pairs such as a glossary or metadata.

questions.text: A recipe lists steps that must be followed in order. Which list element fits best?

options.info: An ordered list <ol> is for items whose sequence matters, like numbered steps; it conveys and can number the order.

options.text: <ul> because all lists are unordered by default
options.info: <ul> is for items whose order is not significant; using it loses the meaning that the steps are sequential.
Plain paragraphs do not express that the items form a list or a sequence.
A description list is for term/description pairs, not for an ordered sequence of steps.

questions.explanation: Choose <ol> when order carries meaning and <ul> when it does not; recipe steps are an ordered list.

questions.text: An <li> element should appear only inside <ul>, <ol> or <menu>.
questions.explanation: A list item <li> must be a child of a list container (<ul>, <ol> or <menu>). On its own it has no valid parent and the list semantics are lost.

options.text:

options.text: A single <span> with a newline character
options.info: <span> is inline and has no block/paragraph meaning; a newline in the source is collapsed to a space by default.

questions.explanation:
Use one

is for meaningful in-line breaks, not for spacing between paragraphs.

questions.text: is appropriate for line breaks that are part of the content, such as lines of a postal address or a poem.
questions.explanation: represents a line break that is meaningful content, like the lines of an address or verse. It should not be used to create vertical spacing between blocks — that is CSS's job.

questions.text: Which element represents a thematic break between paragraph-level sections, such as a scene change in a story?

options.info: <hr> represents a thematic break (a paragraph-level transition), rendered by default as a horizontal rule but meaningful as a content break.
There is no <line> element in HTML.
A CSS border draws a line but conveys no thematic-break meaning to assistive technology.

There is no element in HTML; the line break element is
.

questions.explanation: <hr> is a semantic thematic break, not just a decorative line; a CSS border carries no meaning.

questions.text: You need to target a few words inside a sentence for styling, with no semantic meaning. Which element fits?

options.info: <span> is a generic inline container with no inherent meaning — exactly right for a styling or scripting hook on a run of text.
<div> is a block-level generic container; inside a sentence you need an inline one.
<em> adds stress emphasis (meaning), so it is wrong when you only want to style, not to emphasise.
<mark> means the text is highlighted for relevance; it carries meaning rather than being a neutral hook.

questions.explanation: For a meaningless inline hook use <span>; reach for <em>/<mark> only when you actually mean emphasis or relevance.

questions.text: Reaching for a semantic element before a generic <div> or <span> is good practice when one fits the content.
questions.explanation: The guidance is to use the most meaningful element available; <div> and <span> are fallbacks for when no semantic element fits. Semantic markup gives structure, landmarks and roles for free.

questions.text: Match each element to the partner element it belongs with.
questions.explanation: Several structural elements come in fixed pairs: a figure takes a figcaption, a table takes a caption, a list takes list items, a description list takes terms and descriptions.

questions.text: How many <main> elements should a single page expose to assistive technology?

options.info: There must be only one <main> without the hidden attribute per page; it marks the single primary-content region.
<main> is a page-level region, not a per-section one; multiple visible <main> elements are invalid.
Multiple exposed <main> elements confuse the "main" landmark; the spec allows only one visible at a time.
<body> is the whole document, not the primary-content landmark; <main> marks the primary region specifically.

questions.explanation: A page exposes exactly one <main>. It is the single "skip to main content" target.

questions.text: A page may contain more than one <nav>, for example a primary menu and an in-page table of contents.
questions.explanation: Multiple <nav> regions are allowed. When there are several, give each an accessible name (for example with aria-label) so users can tell the navigation landmarks apart.

questions.text: You are quoting a long passage from another source as its own block. Which element marks it?

options.info: <blockquote> marks an extended quotation set off as its own block, optionally with a cite attribute pointing to the source.
<q> is for a short, inline quotation inside a sentence; it adds quotation marks, not a block.
<cite> names the title of a work, not the quoted passage itself.
Indentation is styling; a <div> gives no quotation semantics.

questions.explanation: A block quotation is <blockquote>; <q> is its short inline sibling, and <cite> names the work, not the quote.

questions.text: You want to show a multi-line code sample that keeps its whitespace and line breaks. Which markup fits?

options.info: <pre> preserves whitespace and line breaks for preformatted text, and <code> inside marks it as computer code — the conventional pairing for code listings.

alone does not preserve whitespace, and
per line is a fragile substitute for 
's formatting.
Faking indentation with   is brittle and conveys no code semantics.
<textarea> is a form control for input; it is not the semantic element for displaying a code sample.

questions.explanation: For a preformatted code block, nest <code> inside <pre>: <pre> keeps the formatting, <code> gives the meaning.

questions.text: <address> is meant for contact information for the nearest <article> or the whole document, not for any postal address on the page.
questions.explanation: <address> marks contact details (email, phone, link) for the author of the nearest article or of the page. A random mailing address in body text is not what it is for.

questions.text: You want a native expandable disclosure widget with a clickable summary. Which elements combine for it?

options.info: <details> is a disclosure widget the user can open and close; its <summary> is the always-visible label that toggles it — no JavaScript required.
A scripted <div> can imitate the behaviour but needs ARIA and keyboard handling to be accessible; <details>/<summary> provide all of that natively.
<dialog> is a modal/non-modal dialog, not an inline expand/collapse disclosure.
<select> is a form dropdown for choosing a value, not a show/hide disclosure of content.

questions.explanation: <details> + <summary> is the native, accessible disclosure pair; it belongs with structural combinatorics because the two always go together.

questions.text: The <summary> element, when present, must be the first child of its <details>.
questions.explanation: If a <details> has a <summary>, it must be the first child; it provides the visible label. Without a <summary>, the browser shows a default label like "Details".

questions.text: You display a published date and want it machine-readable. Which element and attribute fit?

options.info: <time> marks a date or time, and the datetime attribute gives a machine-readable value while the element's text stays human-friendly.
There is no <date> element; the element for dates and times is <time>.
A styled <span> is not machine-readable as a date; <time datetime> provides the parseable value.
There is no <datetime> element; datetime is an attribute of <time>.

questions.explanation: <time> with a datetime attribute is the semantic, machine-readable way to mark a date or time.

questions.text: You need to serve different image sources for different screen widths or formats. Which element coordinates them?

options.info: lets you offer multiple candidates (by media query or type); the required inside is the fallback and the thing actually rendered.
Hiding extra still downloads them and is not the responsive-image mechanism; / let the browser pick one.
<figure> groups captioned content; it does not choose between image sources.
A single src cannot adapt to width or format; that is exactly what <picture> and srcset solve.

questions.explanation: + + a fallback is the responsive-image structure; the is required and is what renders.

questions.text: Every that conveys meaning needs an alt attribute describing it; a purely decorative image should have an empty alt="".
questions.explanation: Meaningful images need descriptive alt text so they are announced; decorative images take alt="" so screen readers skip them. Omitting alt entirely makes some screen readers read the file name.

questions.text: A long data table should group its header row and body rows. Which elements do that?

options.info: <thead> groups the header rows and <tbody> the body rows, which helps structure, styling and (when printed) repeating headers.
<header> and <body> are document-level elements, not table row groups; the table groups are <thead>, <tbody> and <tfoot>.
<top> is not an element, and <main> is a page region, not a table group.
<caption> is the table title and <section> is a page section; neither groups table rows.

questions.explanation: Table rows are grouped with <thead>, <tbody> and optionally <tfoot> — not with document-level elements.

questions.text: Which of these elements expose a landmark role that screen-reader users can jump to? Select every correct answer.

options.info: <nav> exposes the "navigation" landmark.
<main> exposes the "main" landmark.
<aside> exposes the "complementary" landmark.
<span> is a generic inline container with no role at all, so it exposes no landmark.

questions.explanation: <nav>, <main> and <aside> are landmark regions; <span> (like <div>) carries no role and is no landmark.

questions.text: A news homepage shows several independent story teasers, each able to stand alone. How should each teaser be marked?

options.info: Each teaser is self-contained and could be distributed on its own, which is the definition of <article>.
<section> groups related content within a document but does not state that a part is independently distributable.
There is only one <main> per page; it cannot wrap each of many teasers.
The teasers are the main content, not tangential asides.

questions.explanation: Independent, self-contained units are <article>; <section> is for thematic parts that are not necessarily standalone.

questions.text: Giving each <section> and <article> its own heading is what builds a meaningful document outline.
questions.explanation: The outline is formed by the headings inside sectioning elements. A section without a heading has no label in the outline, which makes the document harder to navigate.

questions.text: In a form, you want to group related controls (a set of radio buttons) under a shared caption. Which pair fits?

options.info: <fieldset> groups related form controls and <legend> labels the group, which screen readers announce with each control in it.
A section with a heading groups content but does not give grouped controls a shared, announced legend the way <fieldset>/<legend> do.
A generic div and paragraph give no grouping semantics to the controls.
A table is for tabular data, not for grouping a set of form controls.

questions.explanation: <fieldset> + <legend> is the structural pair for grouping and labelling related form controls — it also belongs in the forms chapter, shown here as structural combinatorics.

questions.text: A <footer> inside an <article> marks the footer of that article, not of the whole page.
questions.explanation: Sectioning context matters: a <footer> (or <header>) nested in an <article> or <section> belongs to that section. Only a top-level <footer> exposes the page's contentinfo landmark.

questions.text: A sentence contains a word that is genuinely important — a safety warning. Which element conveys that importance?

options.info: <strong> marks text with strong importance, seriousness or urgency; its meaning is announced and is not merely visual.
<b> draws attention stylistically (bold) without implying extra importance; it carries no semantic weight for assistive technology.
<big> is a deprecated, obsolete presentational element; use CSS or a semantic element instead.
<mark> means highlighted for relevance to the reader's current activity, not strong importance.

questions.explanation: Use <strong> when the text is important; <b> only bolds without meaning. Meaning beats appearance.

questions.text: You want to stress one word so the sentence's meaning changes, as in "I did not say that." Which element fits?

options.info: <em> marks stress emphasis that changes the meaning of the sentence; a screen reader can convey the emphasis.
<i> marks text in an alternate voice or mood (a term, a thought, a foreign phrase) and is italic by default, but it is not stress emphasis.
<u> is an unarticulated annotation (underline); it is not emphasis.
<cite> names the title of a work, not stressed words.

questions.explanation: <em> is stress emphasis that changes meaning; <i> is an alternate voice with no emphasis. Pick by meaning.

questions.text: <b> and <i> carry no extra importance or emphasis; they only set a visual style that happens to be bold or italic.
questions.explanation: <b> and <i> are presentational-leaning: <b> is stylistically offset text, <i> is an alternate voice or mood. Neither adds the importance of <strong> or the emphasis of <em>, so screen readers do not stress them.

questions.text: You quote one short phrase inside a running sentence. Which element fits?

options.info: <q> marks a short, inline quotation and the browser adds the appropriate quotation marks automatically.
<blockquote> is for an extended quotation set off as its own block, not an inline phrase inside a sentence.
<cite> names the title of a work; it is not the quoted text itself.
<em> is emphasis, not a quotation.

questions.explanation: Short inline quote: <q>; block quote: <blockquote>. The two differ by length and placement.

questions.text: You reference the title of a book in a sentence. Which element marks the title?

options.info: <cite> marks the title of a creative work (book, film, article). It is italic by default but means "title of a work".
<q> marks a short quotation, not the title of a work.
<i> would also render italic, but it does not convey "this is the title of a work" the way <cite> does.
<title> sets the document's title in the browser tab; it is metadata, not inline content.

questions.explanation: <cite> is specifically the title of a work; <i> only looks italic, and <title> is page metadata.

questions.text: You want to show the name of a function inline in a sentence of prose. Which element fits?

options.info: <code> marks a short fragment of computer code inline; it is monospaced by default and tells assistive technology this is code.
<pre> is for preformatted blocks that preserve whitespace, not for a single inline code fragment.
<kbd> marks user keyboard input (keys to press), not a code identifier.
<samp> marks sample output from a program, not a code identifier the author writes.

questions.explanation: Inline code identifier: <code>. <pre> is for blocks, <kbd> is keyboard input, <samp> is program output.

questions.text: Match each code-related element to what it marks.
distractors: The title of a creative work
questions.explanation: The code family splits by role: <code> for code, <kbd> for user input at the keyboard, <samp> for program output, <var> for a variable.

questions.text: You use the abbreviation "HTML" and want to provide its full expansion on hover and to assistive tech. Which element fits?

options.info: <abbr> marks an abbreviation or acronym, and the title attribute gives the full expansion that is shown on hover and can be announced.
<acronym> is a deprecated, obsolete element; <abbr> replaced it for both abbreviations and acronyms.
<dfn> marks the defining instance of a term, not an abbreviation with an expansion.
A span with a title shows a tooltip but does not convey "this is an abbreviation" semantically.

questions.explanation: <abbr title> marks an abbreviation and supplies its expansion; the old <acronym> is obsolete.

questions.text: You show a concert start time and want it machine-readable for calendars. Which element fits?

options.info: <time> with datetime provides a machine-readable date/time while the visible text stays human-friendly.
A custom data- attribute is not a standard machine-readable time; <time datetime> is the semantic choice.
There is no <datetime> element; datetime is an attribute on <time>.
There is no <clock> element in HTML.

questions.explanation: <time datetime> is the semantic, parseable way to mark a point in time.

questions.text: You highlight the search term within a result snippet to show why it matched. Which element fits?

options.info: <mark> marks text highlighted for relevance to the user's current activity, such as a matched search term.
<em> is stress emphasis that changes sentence meaning, not relevance highlighting.
<strong> is strong importance, not "this is relevant to what you searched".
<b> only bolds; it does not express that the text is relevant to the current activity.

questions.explanation: <mark> means highlighted-for-relevance — exactly a matched search term; <em>/<strong>/<b> mean other things.

questions.text: You write a chemical formula like H₂O and a mathematical power like x². Which elements mark the small lower and raised characters?

options.info: <sub> marks subscript (H2O) and <sup> marks superscript (x squared); both carry typographic meaning, not just styling.
<small> marks side comments like fine print; it does not position text as sub- or superscript.
CSS can move the baseline but conveys no sub/superscript meaning to assistive technology; <sub>/<sup> do.
There are no <down> or <up> elements in HTML.

questions.explanation: <sub> and <sup> carry the meaning of subscript and superscript; CSS alone would only move the text visually.

questions.text: <small> is meant for side comments and small print such as legal disclaimers, not merely to make text smaller.
questions.explanation: <small> represents side comments or fine print (copyright, legal text). It happens to render smaller, but its purpose is the meaning; for arbitrary sizing, use CSS.

questions.text: You show an edit: a price was changed. Which elements mark the removed and the added text?

options.text: <del> for removed text and <ins> for inserted text
options.info: <del> marks text removed from the document and <ins> marks text added; together they represent an edit and can carry datetime/cite.
<strike> is a deprecated, obsolete element, and <u> is an underline annotation; neither means "inserted" or "deleted" as an edit.
<s> marks content no longer accurate or relevant; it is not the edit pair, and it cannot mark an insertion.
There are no <remove> or <add> elements in HTML.

questions.explanation: An edit is <del> (removed) and <ins> (added); the old <strike> is obsolete, and <s>/<u> mean different things.

questions.text: A product is marked as no longer available, but it was never an edit to the document. Which element fits the struck-through text?

options.info: <s> marks content that is no longer accurate or relevant (and is not a document edit); it renders with a strikethrough.
<del> specifically means text that was deleted in an edit of the document, which is not the case here.
<strike> is a deprecated, obsolete presentational element replaced by <s> (and by <del> for edits).
<em> is emphasis, unrelated to "no longer relevant".

questions.explanation: No-longer-relevant content is <s>; a tracked document edit is <del>. The obsolete <strike> should not be used.

questions.text: A paragraph introduces and defines a new term for the first time. Which element marks the term being defined?

options.info: <dfn> marks the defining instance of a term — the place where the surrounding text defines it.
<abbr> marks an abbreviation, not the defining instance of a term.
<em> is emphasis; it does not say "this is where the term is defined".
There is no <term> element in HTML; the defining-instance element is <dfn>.

questions.explanation: <dfn> marks the one place a term is defined; later mentions are plain text.

questions.text: <u> is best reserved for non-textual annotations like a misspelling marker, because readers expect underlined text to be a link.
questions.explanation: <u> renders an underline, which readers associate with links, so it is used sparingly — for example to mark a proper name in Chinese or a spelling error — and not just for decoration.

questions.text: A very long URL may need to break onto the next line at a sensible point without a visible hyphen. Which element suggests that break opportunity?

options.info: <wbr> marks a word-break opportunity: a point where the browser may break a line if needed, without forcing a break or adding a hyphen.
forces a line break always, rather than offering an optional one only when needed.
<hr> is a thematic break between blocks, not a word-break opportunity.
A space may wrap but also changes the text; <wbr> adds a break point without inserting any visible character.

questions.explanation:
offers an optional break point;
forces one. For long unbreakable strings, is the tool.

questions.text: You insert a user name of unknown writing direction into a sentence and do not want it to flip the surrounding text's direction. Which element isolates it?

options.info: <bdi> isolates a span of text whose direction might be unknown, so bidirectional reordering does not affect the text around it.
<bdo> overrides the direction of its text explicitly; it does not isolate unknown-direction content the way <bdi> does.
dir="auto" helps detect direction but does not provide the isolation that <bdi> gives against the surrounding text.
There is no <rtl> element in HTML.

questions.explanation: <bdi> isolates text of unknown direction; <bdo> forces a specific direction. They solve different bidi problems.

questions.text: Match each text-level element to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Text-level elements are chosen by meaning: importance, emphasis, relevance, abbreviation — not by how they happen to look.

questions.text: The browser adds the quotation marks for a <q> element, so you should not type them yourself inside it.
questions.explanation: A <q> element is rendered with the appropriate quotation marks by the browser (varying by language). Typing your own would double them up.

questions.text: You want to show pronunciation annotations above East Asian characters. Which element provides that ruby annotation?

options.info: <ruby> represents a ruby annotation, with <rt> giving the small pronunciation text shown above or beside the base characters.
<sup> is generic superscript; it does not provide the ruby base/annotation relationship.
There is no <annotation> element in HTML for this purpose.
<small> is for side comments, not ruby pronunciation annotations.

questions.explanation: Ruby annotations use <ruby> with <rt> (and optionally <rp>); generic superscript does not express the relationship.

questions.text: You quote the exact text a program printed to the screen. Which element marks that sample output?

options.info: <samp> marks sample output from a computer program or system.
<output> is a form-related live result of a calculation, not static sample output quoted in prose.
<code> marks source code, not the program's printed output.
<kbd> marks keys the user presses, not what the program prints.

questions.explanation: Program output quoted in text is <samp>; <output> is a live form result, a different thing.

questions.text: Text inside <pre> preserves spaces and line breaks exactly as written in the source.
questions.explanation: <pre> displays preformatted text: whitespace and newlines are kept as authored, unlike normal flow where runs of whitespace collapse. It is often paired with <code> for code blocks.

questions.text: The HTML spec suggests <b> for things like keywords or product names where you want attention but no added importance. Which statement is right?

options.text: <b> stylistically offsets text without implying importance or emphasis
options.info: <b> draws attention (bold) for keywords, product names or a document lede, but it adds no semantic importance; use <strong> when importance is meant.
They render alike but differ in meaning: <strong> conveys importance, <b> does not.

options.text: <b> is deprecated and must not be used
options.info: <b> is not deprecated; it has a defined (non-semantic) purpose for stylistic offset.
That is <em>; <b> adds no emphasis of meaning.

questions.explanation: <b> is a defined, non-semantic stylistic offset; it is not deprecated, but it is not a synonym for <strong>.

questions.text: You set a foreign-language phrase or a technical term in italics by meaning, not just by style. Which element fits?

options.info: <i> marks text in an alternate voice or mood — a foreign phrase, a technical term, a thought — rendered italic by default.
<em> is stress emphasis that changes the sentence meaning, which is not what a foreign term needs.
<cite> is specifically the title of a work, not a general foreign term.
<dfn> marks the defining instance of a term, not a foreign phrase set in an alternate voice.

questions.explanation: <i> is the alternate-voice italic (foreign phrase, term, thought); <em> would wrongly imply stressed emphasis.

questions.text: Nesting <strong> inside another <strong> increases the relative level of importance of the inner text.
questions.explanation: Each level of nested <strong> raises the relative importance of its contents. This is a defined feature of the element, not just repeated bolding.

questions.text: You show a product name but also want to attach a machine-readable value (a SKU) to it. Which element fits?

options.info: <data> links a piece of content with a machine-readable value in its value attribute, for non-date/time data such as a product code.
<time> is specifically for dates and times; for other machine-readable values use <data>.
<meta> lives in the document <head> as metadata; it does not annotate inline content.
<var> marks a variable name in math or code, not a machine-readable data value.

questions.explanation: <data value> attaches a machine-readable value to inline content; <time> is the date/time-specific variant.

questions.text: You tell the reader to press a keyboard shortcut. Which element marks the keys?

options.info: <kbd> marks user input entered from a keyboard (or another input device), such as a shortcut.
<code> marks source code, not keys the user should press.
<button> is an interactive control, not a way to show which keys to press in prose.
There is no <key> element in HTML; keyboard input is <kbd>.

questions.explanation: Keyboard input is <kbd>; it is distinct from <code> (source code) and <samp> (program output).

questions.text: Which statements correctly contrast a semantic element with its appearance-only lookalike? Select every correct answer.

options.info: <strong> is semantic importance; <b> is a visual offset with no added meaning.

options.text: <em> changes meaning by stress; <i> is an alternate voice without emphasis
options.info: <em> is stress emphasis; <i> marks an alternate voice/mood and does not stress.

options.text: <del> marks a tracked edit; <s> marks content no longer relevant
options.info: <del> is an edit (deletion); <s> is content that is no longer accurate or relevant.

options.text: <mark> and <small> mean exactly the same thing
options.info: <mark> is relevance highlighting and <small> is side comments/fine print; they are unrelated.

questions.explanation: Semantic text elements differ from their visual lookalikes by meaning; <mark> and <small> are not interchangeable.

questions.text: Choosing a text-level element by how it looks (bold, italic) rather than by what it means is a common mistake.
questions.explanation: A frequent error is picking <b>/<i> for bold/italic when the meaning calls for <strong>/<em> (or vice versa). Choose by meaning and let CSS handle appearance.

questions.text: A form calculates a total and you want to show the result in a way assistive tech treats as a live output. Which element fits?

options.info: <output> represents the result of a calculation or user action; it has an implicit live-region behaviour so updates are announced.
<samp> is static sample output quoted in prose, not a live computed form result.
There is no <result> element in HTML; the calculation result element is <output>.
A span with aria-live can work, but <output> is the native, purpose-built element for a calculation result.

questions.explanation: <output> is the native element for a calculation/action result, with live-region semantics built in.

questions.text: Inside a <blockquote>, how should you name the work the quotation comes from?

options.text: A <cite> element with the work's title
options.info: <cite> names the title of the referenced work; it pairs naturally with a quotation to attribute the source.

options.text: The cite attribute is enough and needs no visible text
options.info: The cite attribute holds a URL for machines but is not shown; a visible attribution still uses <cite> text.
There is no <author> element in HTML.
<q> is an inline quotation, not an attribution of the source's title.

questions.explanation: Attribute a quotation's work with <cite>; the cite attribute is a non-visible machine URL, not the visible credit.

questions.text: When bold or italic text also means importance or emphasis, <strong> and <em> are preferred over <b> and <i>.
questions.explanation: If the intent is importance or emphasis, the semantic <strong>/<em> are preferred because their meaning is conveyed to assistive technology; <b>/<i> are for cases with no such meaning.

questions.text: In a formula shown in prose, you mark the letters that stand for variables. Which element fits?

options.info: <var> marks a variable in a mathematical expression or programming context, such as x or n; it is italic by default.
<i> renders italic but does not convey "this is a variable" semantically.
<code> marks code fragments, not specifically a variable placeholder.
<em> is emphasis, not a variable marker.

questions.explanation: A variable in a formula is <var>; <i> only looks italic, and <code> marks code in general.

questions.text: A text input has only placeholder text "Email" and no label. What is the main accessibility problem?

options.text: The placeholder is not a reliable accessible name; the field has no label
options.info: Placeholder text disappears when the user types and is not reliably announced as the field's name. A <label> gives a persistent, announced accessible name.
Placeholders are allowed; the problem is relying on them as a label, not the placeholder itself.

options.text: The input needs an id but no label
options.info: An id alone does not name the control; it is the associated <label> that provides the accessible name.

options.text: Nothing — a placeholder is the same as a label
options.info: A placeholder is a hint, not a label: it vanishes on input and support for announcing it is inconsistent.

questions.explanation: A placeholder is a hint, not a label. Every control needs an associated <label> for a persistent, announced name.

questions.text: Which markup correctly associates a <label> with its text input?

options.info: The label's for attribute matches the input's id, creating an explicit association so clicking the label focuses the input and screen readers announce the name.

options.text: <label>Email</label> then a separate <input> with no link
options.info: Without a for/id match or wrapping, the label and input are not associated; the control has no accessible name.
aria-hidden removes the control from the accessibility tree, and a nearby span does not name it.
The name attribute is for form submission, not for label association; use for/id or wrapping.

questions.explanation: Associate a label explicitly with for matching the input's id (or wrap the input in the label).

questions.text: Wrapping an <input> inside its <label> also associates the two, without needing a for/id pair.
questions.explanation: A label can be associated implicitly by wrapping the control: <label>Email <input type="email"></label>. Clicking the label text then focuses the control, just like the explicit for/id method.

questions.text: A placeholder attribute is a safe replacement for a visible label on a form field.
questions.explanation: It is not: the placeholder disappears once the user types, offers poor colour contrast by default, and is not reliably announced as the field's name. Use a real <label> and treat the placeholder only as an optional hint.

questions.text: A set of radio buttons asks "Preferred contact method". How do you group and caption them?

material.code:
<fieldset>
  <legend>Preferred contact method</legend>
  <label><input type="radio" name="c"> Email</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="c"> Phone</label>
</fieldset>

options.info: <fieldset> groups the related radios and <legend> gives the group a caption that screen readers announce together with each option.
A bold heading in a div does not associate the caption with the group of controls for assistive technology.
One label cannot be the accessible name for several separate controls; a group needs <fieldset>/<legend>.
A section with a heading groups content visually but does not create the control-group/legend relationship.

questions.explanation: Related controls (radios, checkboxes) are grouped with <fieldset> and captioned with <legend>.

questions.text: A dropdown lets the user choose one country from a fixed list. Which elements build it?

options.info: <select> is the dropdown control and each choice is an <option>; the browser provides the open/close and keyboard behaviour natively.
<input list> pairs with a <datalist> for suggestions on a free-text field, which is different from a fixed single-choice dropdown.

options.text: <ul> of <li> links styled as a menu
options.info: A styled list of links is not a form control and does not submit a chosen value natively.
There is no <dropdown> element in HTML; the native dropdown is <select>.

questions.explanation: A single-choice dropdown is <select> with <option> children — native, accessible, keyboard-ready.

questions.text: A long <select> of cities should be grouped under country headings inside the dropdown. Which element groups options?

options.info: <optgroup> groups related <option> elements under a label shown in the dropdown, improving scannability.
<fieldset> groups form controls, not options inside a <select>; it is not valid there.
A <section> is not valid content inside a <select>; use <optgroup>.
Splitting into several selects changes the control; <optgroup> keeps one select but groups its options.

questions.explanation: Group options within a <select> using <optgroup> with a label; other grouping elements are not valid there.

questions.text: You want a free-text field that also offers autocomplete suggestions the user may ignore. Which combination fits?

options.text: <input list="x"> with a <datalist id="x"> of options
options.info: <datalist> provides a list of suggested values linked by the input's list attribute; the user can pick a suggestion or type anything.
<select> restricts the user to the listed choices, whereas the requirement is free text with optional suggestions.
A custom scripted suggestion list reinvents what <datalist> provides natively and must re-create accessibility.
There is no <suggestions> element in HTML; suggestions come from <datalist>.

questions.explanation: Free text with optional suggestions is <input list> + <datalist>; <select> would force a fixed choice.

questions.text: A field should accept an email address and get an email keyboard on phones and basic format checking. Which input type fits?

options.info: type="email" shows an email-optimised keyboard on mobile and lets the browser validate the basic email format.
type="text" works but gives no email keyboard and no built-in format validation.
There is no "mail" input type; the email type is "email".
There is no "string" input type in HTML.

questions.explanation: Pick the input type that matches the data: type="email" gives the right keyboard and validation.

questions.text: A field should accept a whole quantity and offer a numeric keypad with up/down steppers. Which input type fits?

options.info: type="number" accepts numeric input, offers steppers and supports min/max/step for validation.
A pattern can restrict text but does not provide the numeric keypad or steppers that type="number" gives.
type="range" is a slider for approximate values, not for typing an exact quantity.
There is no "digit" input type in HTML.

questions.explanation: Choose type="number" for numeric entry; type="range" is a slider and suits approximate values.

questions.text: You want a native date picker for choosing a calendar date. Which input type fits?

options.info: type="date" provides a native date picker and a machine-readable YYYY-MM-DD value.
type="datetime" was removed from the standard; use type="date", type="time" or type="datetime-local".
There is no "calendar" input type in HTML.
type="text" gives no picker and no date validation; type="date" is purpose-built.

questions.explanation: A calendar date uses type="date"; the old type="datetime" was removed in favour of datetime-local.

questions.text: The user may choose several toppings at once. Which control type fits each topping?

options.info: Checkboxes allow multiple independent selections, which is exactly "choose any number of toppings".
Radio buttons in one group allow only one selection; they are for mutually exclusive choices.
A plain single <select> allows one choice; it would need the multiple attribute, and checkboxes are usually clearer here.
Free text is error-prone for a fixed set of options; checkboxes give a clear multi-select.

questions.explanation: Multiple independent choices use checkboxes; radios are for one-of-a-set. Match the control to the choice model.

questions.text: Radio buttons that belong to the same choice must share the same name attribute so only one can be selected.
questions.explanation: Radios form a group by sharing a name; selecting one deselects the others in that group. Different names would make them behave independently, allowing multiple selections.

questions.text: Inside a <form>, you add a button that must NOT submit the form (it opens a helper panel). Which type prevents submission?

options.info: type="button" is a neutral button that does nothing by default, so it will not submit the form; you attach your own behaviour.
type="submit" submits the form, which is the opposite of what is wanted.
A <button> inside a form defaults to type="submit", so omitting the type would submit the form.
type="reset" clears the form's fields; it also is not a neutral button.

questions.explanation: A <button> in a form defaults to submit; use type="button" for an action that must not submit.

questions.text: A <button> with no type attribute inside a form behaves as a submit button.
questions.explanation: The default type of a <button> is "submit". Forgetting to set type="button" on a non-submitting button is a common cause of forms submitting unexpectedly.

questions.text: You need a control that submits the form when activated. Which element is correct?

options.info: A submit button is the native control that submits a form, with correct keyboard behaviour and the "button" role.
A link has the "link" role and navigates; faking a submit with a link needs scripting and breaks keyboard expectations (Enter vs Space).
A clickable div has no role, is not keyboard-focusable by default, and cannot submit a form natively.
A span with role=button still needs tabindex and key handling and cannot submit a form by itself.

questions.explanation: Submitting a form is a <button>/<input type=submit> job; a link navigates and a div has no role.

questions.text: You need a multi-line free-text comment field. Which element fits?

options.info: <textarea> is the native multi-line text control, with rows/cols and resizing.
A text input is single-line; for multi-line comments use <textarea>.
There is no "longtext" input type in HTML.
A contenteditable div is not a form control, does not submit as a field, and needs extra work to be accessible.

questions.explanation: Multi-line input is <textarea>; <input type=text> is single-line only.

questions.text: A field must be filled before the form can submit, using built-in validation. Which attribute expresses that?

options.info: The required attribute makes the browser block submission and warn the user if the field is empty, with no script needed.
There is no "mandatory" attribute; the constraint attribute is required.
There is no "validate" attribute in HTML forms.
There is no "important" form attribute.

questions.explanation: Native required-field validation uses the required attribute.

questions.text: Match each form element to the element it is normally combined with.
questions.explanation: Form elements come in fixed pairs: a label names an input, a fieldset is captioned by a legend, a select holds options, a datalist feeds an input with a list attribute.

questions.text: A field should hide the characters as the user types a secret. Which input type fits?

options.info: type="password" masks the entered characters, signalling a secret value to the browser and the user.

options.text: type="text" with CSS to hide text
options.info: Styling text to hide it does not give password semantics or secure handling; type="password" is the right control.
There is no "secret" input type in HTML.
type="hidden" is not shown at all; it is for values submitted without user interaction, not for typing a password.

questions.explanation: Secrets use type="password"; type="hidden" is an invisible value the user never edits.

questions.text: A field is a site search box and should get search-specific keyboard and clear button on some browsers. Which input type fits?

options.info: type="search" marks the field as a search box, which some platforms style with a clear control and a search-optimised keyboard.
type="text" works but misses the search semantics and platform affordances of type="search".
There is no "find" input type in HTML.
There is no "query" input type in HTML.

questions.explanation: A search box is type="search" — the type that matches the field's purpose.

questions.text: An <input> with no type attribute defaults to type="text".
questions.explanation: If the type attribute is missing or invalid, an <input> defaults to a single-line text field. Still, setting the correct type gives better keyboards and validation.

questions.text: A phone-number field should bring up a telephone keypad on mobile without enforcing a strict format. Which input type fits?

options.info: type="tel" shows a telephone keypad and does not impose a format, since phone numbers vary worldwide.
type="number" rejects characters like + and spaces and may strip leading zeros, which breaks many phone numbers.
There is no "phone" input type; the telephone type is "tel".
type="text" works but misses the telephone keypad that type="tel" provides.

questions.explanation: Phone numbers use type="tel" (keypad, no strict format); type="number" wrongly strips valid characters.

questions.text: A field should accept a web address and validate its basic URL format. Which input type fits?

options.info: type="url" validates that the value looks like an absolute URL and offers a URL-optimised keyboard.
There is no "link" input type in HTML.
There is no "web" input type in HTML.
type="text" accepts anything with no URL validation; type="url" checks the format.

questions.explanation: A web address field is type="url" for the right keyboard and basic format validation.

questions.text: Every form control that takes user input should have an associated label or an equivalent accessible name.
questions.explanation: Controls need an accessible name so users know what to enter. A visible <label> is best; where a visible label is impossible, an accessible name via aria-label or aria-labelledby is the fallback.

questions.text: The user must upload a document from their device. Which input type fits?

options.info: type="file" lets the user pick one or more files from their device; the accept attribute can restrict file types.
There is no "upload" input type; file selection uses type="file".
There is no "attachment" input type in HTML.
A textarea takes typed text, not an uploaded file.

questions.explanation: File upload is type="file"; use the accept attribute to limit the kinds of file.

questions.text: A form adds two numbers and shows the sum live as the user types. Which element best presents the result?

options.info: <output> is the native element for a calculation result; it has implicit live-region semantics so updates are announced.
A read-only input looks like a field for entry; <output> better conveys "this is a computed result".
A plain paragraph is not announced as a live result and carries no form-result semantics.
A label names a control; it is not where a computed result belongs.

questions.explanation: A live computed form result is <output>; a read-only input or plain paragraph misses the result semantics.

questions.text: Setting the disabled attribute on a <fieldset> disables all the form controls inside it at once.
questions.explanation: A disabled <fieldset> disables every control it contains (except those in its <legend>), which is a convenient way to switch off a whole group of fields.

questions.text: You want a slider for an approximate value like volume, where the exact number is not important. Which input type fits?

options.info: type="range" is a slider for an imprecise value within a min/max; the exact number is less important than the approximate position.
type="number" is for typing an exact value, not a draggable approximate slider.
There is no "slider" input type; the slider is type="range".
There is no "percent" input type in HTML.

questions.explanation: An approximate value uses type="range" (a slider); an exact value uses type="number".

questions.text: Which attributes help the browser and the user fill a field correctly? Select every correct answer.

options.text: autocomplete, to let the browser offer saved values
options.info: autocomplete tells the browser what a field holds (for example "email"), enabling helpful autofill.
required is native validation that stops submission when the field is empty.
Using placeholder as the only label is a bad practice; it should be a hint alongside a real label.

options.text: pattern, to validate the format with a regular expression
options.info: pattern validates the value against a regular expression, with a title describing the expected format.

questions.explanation: autocomplete, required and pattern genuinely help filling and validation; placeholder-as-label does not.

questions.text: You use <input type="submit">. How do you set the button's visible text?

options.info: For <input type="submit">, the value attribute is the button's label; there is no child content.
<input> is a void element with no closing tag, so it cannot hold child text; use the value attribute (or switch to <button>).
There is no label attribute on inputs for this; the submit button's text is its value.
name is the key used on submission, not the visible button text.

questions.explanation: The label of <input type=submit> is its value; <input> cannot hold child text. (<button> can hold rich content.)

questions.text: <button> can contain rich content such as an icon and text, while <input type="button"> can only carry a plain value string.
questions.explanation: A

questions.text: Where must the <legend> appear within a <fieldset>?

options.text: As the first child of the <fieldset>
options.info: The <legend> must be the first child of its <fieldset>; it provides the group's caption.
The legend is required to be first, not last; otherwise it is not a valid caption.
Its position is fixed: it must be the first child to caption the group.
A legend outside its fieldset is not associated with the group.

questions.explanation: The <legend> is the first child of its <fieldset> — that is what captions the control group.

questions.text: You let the user pick a colour with a native colour picker. Which input type fits?

options.info: type="color" opens a native colour picker and returns a hex colour value.
The attribute value is spelled "color" (US spelling); "colour" is not recognised.
There is no "palette" input type in HTML.
A text field gives no colour picker; type="color" is purpose-built.

questions.explanation: A native colour picker is type="color" (US spelling), returning a hex value.

questions.text: A <form> uses the action attribute for the destination URL and the method attribute (GET or POST) for how data is sent.
questions.explanation: The form's action is where the data goes and method is how it is sent. GET appends data to the URL (for safe, idempotent requests); POST sends it in the body (for changes).

questions.text: You must submit a fixed token with the form that the user neither sees nor edits. Which input type fits?

options.info: type="hidden" submits a value with the form without displaying a control, useful for tokens and state.
A password field is visible (masked) and editable; it is not for a fixed, invisible value.

options.text: CSS display:none on a text field
options.info: Hiding a text field with CSS is fragile and still a focusable control; type="hidden" is the intended mechanism.
There is no "secret" input type in HTML.

questions.explanation: A fixed, non-displayed, submitted value is type="hidden" — not a CSS-hidden visible control.

questions.text: Adding the multiple attribute to a <select> lets the user choose more than one option.
questions.explanation: A <select multiple> allows several selections and renders as a list box. For a few independent options, checkboxes are often clearer, but multiple is the native way to multi-select in a <select>.

questions.text: What is the cleanest accessible way to label a single checkbox "I agree to the terms"?

options.text: Wrap the checkbox and text in one <label>
options.info: Wrapping the <input type="checkbox"> and the text in a <label> associates them and makes the whole label clickable to toggle the box.

options.text: Put the text in a <span> next to it with no label
options.info: A nearby span is not associated with the checkbox; the control then has no accessible name.

options.text: Use title on the checkbox only
options.info: A title tooltip is an unreliable accessible name and is not shown as a visible label.
Checkboxes have no placeholder; a label is required to name them.

questions.explanation: Label a checkbox by wrapping it with its text in a <label> (or use for/id); a nearby span is not associated.

questions.text: A developer uses type="number" for a postal code field. Why is that often the wrong choice?

options.text: Postal codes can start with 0 or contain letters/spaces, which type="number" mishandles
options.info: type="number" treats the value as a number: leading zeros and non-digit characters (letters, spaces) are stripped or rejected, breaking many postal codes.
type="number" is not deprecated; it is simply the wrong fit for codes that are not quantities.

options.text: Numbers cannot be submitted in forms
options.info: Numbers submit fine; the issue is that a postal code is an identifier, not a quantity.

options.text: type="number" has no keyboard on mobile
options.info: It does show a numeric keypad; the real problem is losing leading zeros and non-digit characters.

questions.explanation: A postal code is an identifier, not a quantity: use type="text" (with inputmode/pattern), because type="number" drops leading zeros and non-digits.

questions.text: The novalidate attribute on a <form> turns off the browser's built-in validation on submit.
questions.explanation: novalidate disables native constraint validation for the whole form, which is sometimes used when validation is handled entirely in script. Used carelessly, it removes helpful built-in checks.

questions.text: Which button type clears all the form's fields back to their initial values?

options.info: type="reset" resets every control in the form to its initial value. It is used rarely because users often click it by accident.
There is no "clear" button type in HTML; the reset type is "reset".
type="submit" sends the form; it does not clear it.
type="button" does nothing by default; resetting the form is type="reset".

questions.explanation: Resetting a form is type="reset"; use it sparingly, as accidental clicks lose the user's input.

questions.text: Which input type choices match their data well? Select every correct answer.

options.info: type="email" gives an email keyboard and basic format validation.
type="date" provides a date picker and a machine-readable value.

options.text: type="number" for a house number that may include letters
options.info: House numbers like "12b" contain letters, which type="number" rejects; use type="text".
type="tel" offers a phone keypad without forcing a strict numeric format.

questions.explanation: Match the type to the data: email, date and tel fit; a house number with letters does not belong in type="number".

questions.text: You want a native, no-JavaScript expand/collapse section (an FAQ answer). Which elements fit?

material.code:
How do I reset my password?

Use the “Forgot password” link.

options.info: <details> is a disclosure widget the user toggles open and closed; <summary> is the always-visible, clickable label. No JavaScript is needed.
<dialog> is a modal or non-modal dialog box, not an inline expand/collapse section.
A scripted div must re-create the toggling, keyboard support and ARIA that <details>/<summary> provide natively.
There is no <accordion> element in HTML; the native disclosure is <details>/<summary>.

questions.explanation: A native disclosure is <details> + <summary>; it needs no script and is accessible by default.

questions.text: You want a native modal dialog that traps focus and dims the page behind it. Which element and method fit?

options.info: <dialog> is the native dialog element; showModal() opens it as a modal, with a ::backdrop and built-in focus handling.
<details> is an inline disclosure, not a modal dialog; it does not trap focus or dim the page.
A fixed div must re-create modal behaviour (focus trap, Escape, backdrop, aria-modal); <dialog>/showModal() provides it natively.
There is no <modal> element in HTML; the native dialog is <dialog>.

questions.explanation: A native modal is <dialog> with showModal(); it brings focus handling and a backdrop that a plain div lacks.

questions.text: Calling showModal() on a <dialog> opens it as a modal that disables interaction with the rest of the page, while show() opens it non-modally.
questions.explanation: showModal() opens a modal dialog (page behind is inert, a backdrop appears, Escape closes it); show() opens it as a non-modal dialog that leaves the rest of the page interactive.

questions.text: You wrap a site's search form so assistive tech recognises it as the search landmark. Which element fits?

options.info: <search> is the semantic container for search and filtering controls; it exposes the "search" landmark role natively.
This works via ARIA, but the native <search> element is the modern, cleaner way to get the search landmark.
<nav> is the navigation landmark, not search; a search form is not primarily navigation links.
A plain <form> has the generic "form" role, not the "search" landmark; wrap it in <search> for that.

questions.explanation: The native search landmark is the <search> element; previously you added role="search" to a container.

questions.text: You want a lightweight popover (a hint card) that the browser shows and light-dismisses natively, without a dialog. What provides this?

options.text: The popover attribute plus a button with popovertarget
options.info: The popover attribute turns an element into a popover; a <button popovertarget="id"> toggles it, and the browser handles top-layer rendering and light dismiss natively.
There is no <popover> element; popover is a global attribute applied to an existing element (often a <div>).
<dialog> is for dialogs; the popover attribute is the lighter mechanism for popovers and menus with light dismiss.
There is no <tooltip> element in HTML.

questions.explanation: Popovers come from the popover attribute (plus popovertarget on a button), not from a <popover> element — a common misconception.

questions.text: "popover" is a global HTML attribute, not an element; you apply it to an element such as a <div>.
questions.explanation: The Popover API is driven by the popover global attribute and the popovertarget attribute on a button. There is no <popover> element; distinguishing feature-as-attribute from feature-as-element is a common point of confusion.

questions.text: MDN now lists an experimental <geolocation> element. How does it differ from the older navigator.geolocation JavaScript API?

options.text: <geolocation> is an HTML element that renders a share-location control; navigator.geolocation is a JS-only API with no element
options.info: The experimental <geolocation> element creates an interactive control for the user to share their location, with a consistent built-in UI and permission flow; the older Geolocation API is pure JavaScript (navigator.geolocation) with no element of its own.

options.text: They are the same thing with two names
options.info: They are different mechanisms: one is a new HTML element, the other a long-standing JS API; the element aims to solve some of the API's UX shortcomings.

options.text: <geolocation> is a JS API and navigator.geolocation is an element
options.info: It is the other way round: <geolocation> is the element, navigator.geolocation is the JS API.

options.text: Neither exists in HTML or JS
options.info: Both exist: navigator.geolocation is established, and <geolocation> is a new experimental element on MDN.

questions.explanation: The <geolocation> element is HTML with a rendered control; navigator.geolocation is a pure JS API. Telling element from JS-only API is the key skill here.

questions.text: Which of these are real HTML elements (not pure JavaScript APIs)? Select every correct answer.

options.info: <dialog> is a real HTML element for dialog boxes.
<details> is a real HTML element, a native disclosure widget.
fetch() is a JavaScript API for network requests; it has no HTML element.
<search> is a real HTML element exposing the search landmark.

questions.explanation: <dialog>, <details> and <search> are real elements; fetch() is a JS-only API with no element — that is the distinction to keep.

questions.text: You show how far a file upload has progressed toward completion. Which element fits?

options.info: <progress> shows the completion progress of a task, with value and max attributes; it is announced as a progress indicator.
<meter> shows a scalar measurement within a known range (like disk usage), not task progress toward completion.
There is no <range> element; a slider is <input type="range">, which is a control, not a progress display.
A styled div needs ARIA (role, aria-valuenow) to be announced; <progress> provides this natively.

questions.explanation: Task completion is <progress>; a gauge of a measurement within a range is <meter>. They are not the same.

questions.text: You display a gauge of current disk usage within its known minimum and maximum. Which element fits?

options.info: <meter> represents a scalar measurement within a known range (a gauge), with value, min, max and optional low/high/optimum.
<progress> indicates how far a task has advanced, not a static gauge reading within a range.
There is no <gauge> element in HTML; the gauge is <meter>.
<output> is a calculation result; it is not a gauge within a known range.

questions.explanation: A gauge within a known range is <meter>; <progress> is for task completion over time.

questions.text: In a customizable select, which modern element mirrors the chosen option's content inside the button part?

options.info: <selectedcontent> is a new element used with customizable <select> to reflect the currently selected option's content in the button; it is part of recent, limited-availability work.
selected is an attribute on <option>, not an element; the element here is <selectedcontent>.
That marks an option as pre-selected; it does not mirror the selection into the select's button display.
There is no <chosen> element in HTML.

questions.explanation: <selectedcontent> is the modern element that reflects the chosen option in a customizable select; it is new and of limited availability.

questions.text: Giving several <details> elements the same name attribute makes them behave as an exclusive accordion, where opening one closes the others.
questions.explanation: The name attribute on <details> groups them: only one in the group can be open at a time, so opening one closes the rest — a native accordion without script.

questions.text: What is a built-in way for a user to dismiss a modal <dialog> opened with showModal()?

options.info: A modal dialog can be closed by pressing Escape; this behaviour is provided by the element without extra code.

options.text: Clicking anywhere on the page body behind it
options.info: A modal blocks interaction with the page behind it; a click on the inert background does not close it by default.
Scrolling does not dismiss a modal dialog.
Escape (or a close button/form method=dialog) closes it; reloading is not required.

questions.explanation: A modal <dialog> closes on Escape natively; the inert background behind it does not dismiss it on click.

questions.text: Inside a <dialog>, how can a form close the dialog and report which button was pressed, without JavaScript?

options.info: A form with method="dialog" closes the dialog on submit and sets its returnValue to the submitting button's value — all natively.
A link navigates; it does not close a dialog or report a return value.
Reset clears fields; it does not close the dialog.
method="dialog" makes it possible without script.

questions.explanation: method="dialog" lets a form close the <dialog> and record the chosen button — native, no script.

questions.text: Adding the open attribute to a <details> makes it start in the expanded state.
questions.explanation: The boolean open attribute causes a <details> to render open on load. Removing it (the default) starts the disclosure collapsed.

questions.text: You need to draw and update bitmap graphics (a game scene) with JavaScript. Which element provides the drawing surface?

options.info: <canvas> is a bitmap drawing surface controlled with the Canvas or WebGL JavaScript APIs; it holds no inherent structure, so you must provide accessible fallback content.
<svg> is vector graphics with a DOM; <canvas> is the right fit specifically for scripted bitmap drawing such as a game scene.
There is no <draw> element in HTML.
displays a fixed image; it is not a surface you draw on with script.

questions.explanation: Scripted bitmap drawing uses <canvas>; provide fallback content inside it, because it exposes no structure to assistive tech.

questions.text: Because a <canvas> is just a pixel surface, you should provide accessible fallback content or an alternative for its meaning.
questions.explanation: A canvas has no semantic structure of its own, so content drawn on it is invisible to assistive technology. You must supply fallback content inside the element or an accessible alternative for what it conveys.

questions.text: You embed another page with an <iframe>. What makes it understandable to screen-reader users?

options.text: A descriptive title attribute on the <iframe>
options.info: The title attribute gives the embedded frame an accessible name, so users know what the frame contains before entering it.
<iframe> has no alt attribute; its accessible name comes from the title attribute.
Without a title, a frame is announced generically, which is confusing when there are several frames.
<iframe> has no placeholder; use title to name it.

questions.explanation: Name an <iframe> with a descriptive title attribute (not alt, which it does not have).

questions.text: You add captions to a <video> for deaf and hard-of-hearing users. Which element provides the timed caption file?

options.info: <track> adds timed text (captions, subtitles, descriptions) to <video> or <audio>; kind="captions" marks it as captions.
<caption> is the title of a table, not timed text for media.
There is no <subtitles> element; timed text uses <track>.
A paragraph of text is not synchronised with the media; <track> provides timed captions.

questions.explanation: Timed captions for media come from <track> (kind="captions"); <caption> is for tables, a different thing.

questions.text: Providing a text transcript or captions for <audio> and <video> content improves accessibility.
questions.explanation: Media alone excludes users who cannot hear or see it. Captions (via <track>) and a transcript make the content available to deaf, hard-of-hearing and other users, and help everyone in noisy or quiet settings.

questions.text: You want inert HTML in the document that is not rendered until you clone it with JavaScript. Which element holds it?

options.info: <template> holds HTML that is parsed but not rendered or activated; scripts clone its content to instantiate it when needed.
