Stuffing markup in a script tag is an older hack; <template> is the native, purpose-built inert-content element.
A hidden div is still rendered (just not shown) and its contents are active, for example images load; <template> content is truly inert.
There is no <fragment> element in HTML; inert template content is <template>.

questions.explanation: Inert, not-yet-rendered markup for cloning is <template>; a hidden div still activates its contents.

questions.text: Inside a web component's shadow DOM, which element marks a placeholder where the component's light-DOM children are projected?

options.info: <slot> is a placeholder inside a shadow tree that the component fills with the user's light-DOM content, enabling composition.
There is no <insert> element; the void inserted/deleted text element is <ins>, unrelated to slotting.
<content> was part of an obsolete version of the spec; the current projection element is <slot>.
There is no <placeholder> element in HTML.

questions.explanation: Web-component content projection uses <slot>; the old <content> element is obsolete.

questions.text: A custom element defined via the Custom Elements API must have a hyphen in its tag name, such as <my-widget>.
questions.explanation: Custom element names must contain a hyphen to avoid clashing with current and future standard elements. This is why <my-widget> is valid but <mywidget> is not a valid custom element name.

questions.text: A cookie notice must appear on top of the page and block interaction until the user chooses. Which is the better fit?

options.info: A blocking, on-top notice is a modal dialog; <dialog> with showModal() renders in the top layer, traps focus and dims the page.
<details> is an inline, non-blocking disclosure; it does not sit on top of the page or trap focus.
A section in normal flow does not block interaction or appear in the top layer.
<aside> is complementary content in the flow, not a blocking overlay.

questions.explanation: A blocking overlay is a modal <dialog>; <details> is only an inline expand/collapse.

questions.text: A <summary> is placed outside of any <details>. What happens to its disclosure behaviour?

options.text: It loses its disclosure meaning; <summary> only works as the first child of <details>
options.info: <summary> is defined as the label and toggle of its parent <details>; outside a <details> it has no disclosure behaviour.
There is nothing for a lone <summary> to toggle; its behaviour comes from its <details> parent.
<summary> is not a heading; it is the caption of a disclosure widget.

options.text: It becomes a button that submits forms
options.info: <summary> does not submit forms; its role is tied to <details>.

questions.explanation: <summary> only has meaning as the first child of <details>; on its own it toggles nothing.

questions.text: Which of these are modern, real HTML features rather than purely JavaScript APIs? Select every correct answer.

options.info: popover is a real HTML global attribute (with popovertarget) that drives native popovers.
<search> is a real HTML element exposing the search landmark.
localStorage is a JavaScript storage API; it has no HTML element or attribute.
<dialog> is a real HTML element for dialogs.

questions.explanation: popover, <search> and <dialog> are real HTML; localStorage is a JS-only API. Keep element/attribute features apart from JS APIs.

questions.text: Using the native <dialog> element is generally preferable to building a modal from a <div>, because it provides focus management and a backdrop for free.
questions.explanation: The native <dialog> gives top-layer rendering, a ::backdrop, focus trapping and Escape-to-close without custom code, which a hand-built <div> modal must re-implement and often gets wrong.

questions.text: You want to show a message only when the user's browser has JavaScript disabled. Which element fits?

options.info: <noscript> shows its content only when scripting is disabled (or unsupported), a native fallback mechanism.
There is no fallback attribute on <script>; the no-script fallback element is <noscript>.
If script is disabled, a script-toggled div cannot reveal itself; <noscript> handles the no-JS case natively.
There is no <fallback> element in HTML.

questions.explanation: No-JavaScript fallback content is <noscript>; a script-toggled div cannot work when script is off.

questions.text: You want clickable regions on a single image (an image map). Which elements define the regions?

options.info: defines an image map referenced by an , and each is a clickable region with its own shape, coordinates and accessible name.
There is no <region> element; image-map regions are <area> inside a <map>.

options.text: Several overlapping <a> over the image with CSS
options.info: Overlaying links works but is not the native image-map mechanism; <map>/<area> is purpose-built and each area needs alt text.
There is no <hotspot> element in HTML.

questions.explanation: An image map is <map> + <area>; give each <area> an alt text for accessibility.

questions.text: The <geolocation> element is an experimental proposal and should not be relied on in production yet.
questions.explanation: The <geolocation> element is new and experimental, with limited availability across browsers as of late 2025. Treat it as a proposal to watch, not a feature to depend on in production.

questions.text: A control triggers an in-page action (opens a menu) and goes nowhere. An <a href="#"> is used with a click handler. What is the correct element?

options.info: An in-page action is a button: <button> has the "button" role, is keyboard-operable with Space and Enter, and needs no href.
A link has the "link" role and is meant to navigate; href="#" also jumps to the top. It confuses screen-reader users expecting navigation and uses the wrong key behaviour.
A clickable div has no role and is not focusable by default; it needs tabindex and key handlers to approximate a button.
role="link" announces a link, which is wrong for an action, and it still needs tabindex and key handling.

questions.explanation: Action = <button>; navigation = <a href>. A link that performs an action should be a button.

questions.text: A control takes the user to another page at /about. Which element is correct?

options.info: Navigation to a URL is a link: <a href> has the "link" role, works with the keyboard, supports open-in-new-tab, and is crawlable.
A scripted button can navigate but loses link affordances (middle-click, right-click menu, status bar, crawlability) and misstates the role.
A clickable div is neither a link nor keyboard-focusable by default.
A button role is wrong for navigation; and it still lacks native link behaviour.

questions.explanation: Navigation to a URL is an <a href>; a scripted button throws away everything links give you for free.

questions.text: An <a> element without an href attribute does not get the link role and is not keyboard-focusable by default.
questions.explanation: A link is only a link (and focusable) when it has an href. An <a> with no href is a placeholder with no role; for an action, use a <button> instead.

questions.text: Match each element to its implicit ARIA role.
questions.explanation: Native elements come with implicit ARIA roles: a button is "button", a link "link", a nav "navigation", an unordered list "list". Using them means you rarely need to set role yourself.

questions.text: Match each element to its implicit ARIA role.
questions.explanation: <main> is the "main" landmark, a checkbox input is "checkbox", a heading carries a heading role with its level, and an image with alt is "img". These roles are built in.

questions.text: A developer adds role="button" to a native <button>. Is that a good idea?

options.text: No — it is redundant; the <button> already has the button role
options.info: A <button> already exposes the "button" role. Adding role="button" is redundant and risks overriding or clashing with native semantics — “No ARIA is better than bad ARIA”.
Roles are not strengthened by repetition; the native role is already present, so the attribute adds nothing useful.

options.text: Yes — ARIA is always required on interactive elements
options.info: ARIA is not required on elements that already carry the right native semantics; prefer native HTML.

options.text: No — because role is not a valid attribute
options.info: role is valid, but here it is simply redundant on an element that already has that role.

questions.explanation: Native semantics win: do not re-declare a role an element already has. No ARIA is better than bad ARIA.

questions.text: If a native HTML element with the needed semantics exists, it is preferable to re-creating the behaviour on a generic element with ARIA.
questions.explanation: The first rule of ARIA is to use a native element or attribute with the semantics and behaviour you need instead of repurposing a <div>/<span> with a role. Native elements bring keyboard support and state handling for free.

questions.text: Someone builds a button as <div role="button" tabindex="0"> with a click handler. What is still missing compared with a real <button>?

options.text: Keyboard activation with Enter and Space must be added by hand
options.info: A real <button> fires on Enter and Space automatically; the div version needs a keydown handler to match, which is easy to get wrong — another reason to prefer <button>.
It is not equivalent: native keyboard activation and form participation are missing and must be re-created.
Styling is not the accessibility gap; keyboard and semantics are.
Buttons do not use href; the missing piece is native keyboard activation and semantics.

questions.explanation: A div with role=button still lacks native Enter/Space handling and form behaviour; a real <button> has them.

questions.text: An icon-only button shows a magnifier glyph and no text. How do you give it an accessible name?

options.info: An icon-only control needs an accessible name; aria-label provides one, as does visually hidden text inside the button. Otherwise screen readers announce an unnamed button.

options.text: Rely on the title of the icon image
options.info: A decorative glyph often has no reliable name; aria-label (or hidden text) is the dependable way to name the control.
A glyph alone is not announced as a name, leaving the button unlabeled for screen-reader users.
Buttons have no placeholder; name them with text or aria-label.

questions.explanation: Name an icon-only button with aria-label or visually hidden text; a bare glyph is not an accessible name.

questions.text: A decorative image that adds no information should have an empty alt (alt="") so screen readers skip it.
questions.explanation: An empty alt marks an image as decorative, so assistive technology ignores it. Omitting alt entirely is different: some screen readers then announce the file name, which is noise.

questions.text: Why do screen-reader users rely on a correct heading structure (<h1>–<h6>)?

options.text: They can jump between headings to scan and navigate the page
options.info: Screen readers let users list and jump between headings; a logical, unskipped hierarchy is one of the main ways they understand and move through a page.

options.text: Headings change the text colour for low vision
options.info: Colour is a CSS concern; the accessibility value of headings is the navigable outline they create.

options.text: Headings are required for the page to load
options.info: Pages load without headings; the benefit is navigation and structure, not loading.
Headings have nothing to do with form submission.

questions.explanation: Headings give screen-reader users a navigable outline to jump through; keep levels logical and unskipped.

questions.text: Associating a <label> with an <input> does what for accessibility?

options.text: Gives the control an accessible name and makes the label clickable to focus it
options.info: A proper label provides the control's accessible name (announced by screen readers) and lets users click the label text to focus or toggle the control, enlarging the hit area.
A label does not change the input type; it names the control.
A label does not submit anything; it labels a control.
Validation comes from attributes like required/pattern, not from the label.

questions.explanation: A label gives the control its accessible name and a clickable target — core form accessibility.

questions.text: Removing the focus outline from interactive elements without providing an equally visible alternative harms keyboard accessibility.
questions.explanation: The focus indicator tells keyboard users where they are. Removing it (for example outline:none) with no visible replacement leaves keyboard and switch users unable to track focus, which fails accessibility expectations.

questions.text: You need a normally non-focusable element to receive keyboard focus in the natural tab order. Which value fits?

options.info: tabindex="0" puts an element into the natural tab order at its DOM position, making it focusable without jumping the order.
Positive tabindex values force a custom tab order that overrides the DOM order and is widely discouraged as error-prone.
tabindex="-1" makes an element focusable by script but removes it from the tab order, so Tab will not reach it.
There is no "auto" value for tabindex.

questions.explanation: tabindex="0" adds an element to the natural order; positive values are discouraged, and -1 removes it from tabbing.

questions.text: What does a "skip to main content" link let keyboard and screen-reader users do?

options.text: Bypass repeated navigation and jump straight to <main>
options.info: A skip link, usually the first focusable element, lets users jump past repeated header/navigation to the main content — a common pairing with a well-marked <main>.
A skip link moves focus; it does not change what loads.
It navigates focus to a target, not submitting anything.
Language is set with the lang attribute, unrelated to skip links.

questions.explanation: A skip link jumps past repeated navigation to the main content; it pairs with a clearly marked <main>.

questions.text: Setting the lang attribute on <html> helps screen readers pronounce the page in the correct language.
questions.explanation: The lang attribute declares the content's language so assistive technology uses the right pronunciation and voice. A section in another language can carry its own lang to switch correctly.

questions.text: A navigation menu is marked up as a <ul> of <li> links. What implicit roles do the list and its items expose?

options.info: A <ul> has the implicit role "list" and each <li> has "listitem"; screen readers can announce the number of items, which helps users orient.
menu/menuitem are roles for application-style menus (menu widgets), not the default for a plain <ul>/<li>.
The navigation landmark comes from <nav>, and link from each <a>; the list itself is list/listitem.
group/option are for listbox-style widgets, not a plain list.

questions.explanation: A <ul>/<li> exposes list/listitem; wrapping it in <nav> adds the navigation landmark separately.

questions.text: Why mark column and row headers with <th> and scope in a data table?

options.text: So screen readers announce the relevant header with each data cell
options.info: Proper <th> and scope let assistive technology tie each data cell to its headers, so a user hears “Price: 12” instead of a disconnected “12”.

options.text: To make the table load faster
options.info: Headers do not affect load speed; they affect how the data is understood without sight.
Styling is CSS; <th> is about semantics and header association.
<th> does not sort; it identifies header cells for accessibility and structure.

questions.explanation: Header cells with scope let a cell be announced with its headers — the core of accessible data tables.

questions.text: Applying aria-hidden="true" to an element removes it and its subtree from the accessibility tree, so screen readers ignore it.
questions.explanation: aria-hidden="true" hides content from assistive technology while leaving it visible. It is useful for decorative duplicates but dangerous on anything meaningful or focusable, which would then be unreachable or confusing.

questions.text: How does wrapping radio buttons in <fieldset> with a <legend> help screen-reader users?

options.text: The legend is announced as the group's question with each option
options.info: The <legend> provides a group label that assistive technology associates with every control in the fieldset, so each radio is announced in the context of the question.
Size is styling; the accessibility benefit is the announced group label.
Grouping does not validate; it provides a shared accessible context.
Grouping does not change the control type.

questions.explanation: <fieldset>/<legend> give grouped controls a shared, announced question — vital context for the options.

questions.text: Several links on a page all read "click here". Why is this an accessibility problem?

options.text: Out of context, the link purpose is unclear when links are listed or read alone
options.info: Screen-reader users often navigate a list of links out of context; “click here” repeated gives no clue where each goes. Link text should describe its destination.
It is not reserved; the issue is that it is not descriptive out of context.

options.text: Links must never contain the word "here"
options.info: There is no such rule; the point is descriptive, self-explaining link text.
It is a comprehension problem, not a performance one.

questions.explanation: Link text must make sense out of context; repeated “click here” tells screen-reader users nothing about the destination.

questions.text: Conveying information by colour alone (for example a red field means error) can exclude users who cannot perceive the colour difference.
questions.explanation: Colour should not be the only means of conveying information. Pair it with text, an icon or a pattern so colour-blind and low-vision users get the same message.

questions.text: What implicit role does <input type="checkbox"> expose?

options.info: A checkbox input exposes the "checkbox" role and a checked state, both handled natively.
textbox is the role of a text input; a checkbox has the "checkbox" role.
A checkbox is not a button; its role is "checkbox".
A switch is a different role; a plain checkbox is "checkbox" (though role=switch can be added deliberately).

questions.explanation: <input type=checkbox> is the "checkbox" role with native checked state — no ARIA needed.

questions.text: A page has two <nav> regions (primary and footer). How do you help users tell them apart?

options.text: Give each an accessible name, e.g. aria-label="Primary" and aria-label="Footer"
options.info: When several landmarks of the same type exist, naming each (aria-label or aria-labelledby) lets users distinguish them in the landmarks list.
Both navigations are legitimate; naming them is the fix, not deleting one.
Dropping to a div loses the navigation landmark; keep <nav> and name them.
Two unnamed navigation landmarks are hard to tell apart; naming is recommended.

questions.explanation: Multiple same-type landmarks should each get an accessible name so users can distinguish them.

questions.text: aria-label can override the visible text of an element, so it should be used carefully and never to hide the visible label from screen readers.
questions.explanation: aria-label replaces an element's accessible name with its value. Set carelessly on an element that already has visible text, it can make the announced name differ from what sighted users see, which is confusing.

questions.text: How does the native required attribute help accessibility compared with only a red asterisk?

options.text: It conveys the required state to assistive technology, which announces it
options.info: required exposes the field's required state so screen readers announce it; a red asterisk alone is only visual and may be missed.
required does not style the field; it conveys state and triggers validation.
required blocks submission when empty; it does not submit.
required does not label the field; it marks it as mandatory.

questions.explanation: required conveys the mandatory state to assistive tech, unlike a purely visual asterisk.

questions.text: A screen-reader user wants to jump straight to the page's primary content. Which element makes that possible as a landmark?

options.info: <main> exposes the "main" landmark, which assistive technology offers as a direct jump target for the primary content.
A div exposes no landmark, so there is nothing to jump to; use <main>.
<article> marks a self-contained unit, not the single primary-content landmark of the page.
<section> is a generic region, not the "main" landmark.

questions.explanation: The jump-to-content landmark is <main>; a plain div gives screen-reader users nothing to target.

questions.text: Native interactive elements like <button>, <a href> and form controls are keyboard-operable by default, which custom <div> widgets are not.
questions.explanation: Native controls come with focusability and keyboard behaviour built in. A custom widget built from <div>/<span> must add tabindex and key handling to match, which is extra work that is easy to get wrong.

questions.text: For a chart image in a <figure>, what is the right division between alt text and <figcaption>?

options.text: alt describes the image's content for non-sighted users; figcaption is a visible caption for everyone
options.info: The alt conveys what the image shows to those who cannot see it; the <figcaption> is a visible caption shown to all. They complement each other rather than duplicate.
Identical text is redundant; alt and caption serve different audiences and purposes.

options.text: Only the caption matters; alt can be empty for meaningful images
options.info: A meaningful image still needs alt; an empty alt is only for decorative images.

options.text: alt should contain the licence text
options.info: Licence and source belong in the figure's credit, not in alt, which describes the content.

questions.explanation: alt describes the content for non-sighted users; figcaption is a visible caption for all — they complement, not duplicate.

questions.text: Content updates dynamically (a status message) and should be announced without moving focus. Which approach fits, preferring native where possible?

options.text: Use <output> or an element with aria-live for the status region
options.info: <output> has an implicit live region, and aria-live="polite" can mark any region so updates are announced without stealing focus.

options.text: Move focus to the message each time
options.info: Forcibly moving focus interrupts the user; a live region announces updates without a focus jump.
Rewriting the title is not a reliable status-announcement mechanism and is disruptive.
Dynamic updates are not announced unless the region is a live region (native <output> or aria-live).

questions.explanation: Announce dynamic updates with a live region — native <output> or aria-live — instead of grabbing focus.

questions.text: Setting role="list" on a <ul> is normally unnecessary because <ul> already has the list role.
questions.explanation: A <ul> already exposes the list role, so role="list" is usually redundant. (One narrow exception: some CSS that removes list styling can strip the role in certain browsers, where authors restore it deliberately.)

questions.text: What is wrong with putting an <a href> inside a <button> (or a <button> inside an <a>)?

options.text: Interactive elements must not be nested; the roles and activation conflict
options.info: Nesting interactive controls is invalid and produces conflicting roles and unpredictable keyboard/activation behaviour. Keep a link and a button as separate controls.
It is not valid; interactive content may not contain other interactive content like this.
The problem is semantic and behavioural, not merely visual.

options.text: The button becomes a link automatically
options.info: It does not merge roles; it creates an invalid, conflicting structure.

questions.explanation: Do not nest interactive elements (a link in a button or vice versa); it is invalid and conflicts in role and activation.

questions.text: In which cases does native HTML already give the accessibility you need, so extra ARIA is unnecessary? Select every correct answer.

options.info: <button> already has the button role and keyboard activation; no ARIA needed.
<a href> has the link role and keyboard support natively.
<nav> exposes the navigation landmark without any ARIA.

options.text: A <div> you want to behave like a button
options.info: A div needs role, tabindex and key handling to act as a button — better to use a real <button>.

questions.explanation: Native <button>, <a href> and <nav> bring their semantics for free; only the custom div needs ARIA (and is best avoided).

questions.text: What implicit role does a <select> (without multiple) expose?

options.info: A single-choice <select> exposes the "combobox" role (a collapsible list of options); its options expose "option".
list is the role of a <ul>; a <select> is a combobox (or listbox with multiple).
menu is an application-menu role, not the role of a form <select>.
textbox is for text entry; a <select> is a combobox.

questions.explanation: A single <select> is a "combobox"; its options are "option". Native roles come built in.

questions.text: An icon that sits next to a visible text label and only decorates it can be hidden from screen readers with aria-hidden="true".
questions.explanation: When the adjacent text already conveys the meaning, the icon is decorative and can be hidden with aria-hidden="true" to avoid a redundant or confusing announcement.

questions.text: A designer uses <h3> for a line of text only because the default size looks right, though it is not a section title. What is the accessibility concern?

options.text: It adds a false entry to the heading outline, misleading screen-reader navigation
options.info: Choosing a heading for its size inserts a heading into the outline that is not really a section title, which misleads users who navigate by headings. Style with CSS instead.
Headings can be styled; the issue is using heading markup purely for its default size.
It harms the outline; headings are structural, not sizing tools.
The real problem is the misleading outline, not layout.

questions.explanation: Headings build the outline; using one just for its size injects a false structural entry. Choose by meaning, size with CSS.

questions.text: How does a <caption> improve a data table's accessibility?

options.text: It gives the table an accessible name announced when the user enters it
options.info: <caption> is the table's title and is announced as its accessible name, so a screen-reader user knows what the table is about before exploring cells.
A caption does not sort; it names the table.
A caption does not affect headers; it titles the table.
It is semantic: the announced table title, not decoration.

questions.explanation: A <caption> is the table's announced name — context a screen-reader user hears on entering the table.

questions.text: Adding a wrong ARIA role to a native element can override its correct built-in role and make it less accessible.
questions.explanation: ARIA roles override native semantics. Putting role="presentation" on a table or a wrong role on a control can strip meaning that users depend on — which is why incorrect ARIA is worse than none.

questions.text: What does it mean when a web feature is "Baseline widely available"?

options.text: It has worked across the major browsers for a good while and is safe to use broadly
options.info: Baseline “widely available” means the feature has been interoperable across the core browser set for about 30 months, so it is a safe default for most projects.

options.text: It works only in one browser
options.info: Single-browser support is the opposite of Baseline; widely available means broad, interoperable support.

options.text: It is experimental and may be removed
options.info: Experimental is a separate status; widely available means stable and broadly supported.
Deprecated means discouraged/being removed, not widely available.

questions.explanation: Baseline “widely available” = interoperable across major browsers for a long time, a safe default.

questions.text: A feature is "Baseline newly available". What does that tell you?

options.text: It has just become interoperable across the major browsers; check whether your audience is up to date
options.info: “Newly available” means the feature reached interoperability across the core browsers recently; it is usable, but older browser versions in the wild may still lack it.

options.text: It only works in nightly builds
options.info: Nightly-only is pre-availability; newly available means it has shipped across the core browsers.

options.text: It will never be widely available
options.info: Newly available features typically progress to widely available over time.
Newly available is the opposite of obsolete; it is recent, supported work.

questions.explanation: “Newly available” = recently interoperable across core browsers; fine to use, but mind older installed versions.

questions.text: A feature shows "limited availability" (not yet Baseline). How should you treat it?

options.text: Use it with care and a fallback; support is still uneven across browsers
options.info: Limited availability means the feature is not yet interoperable everywhere, so it needs feature detection and a fallback for browsers that lack it.

options.text: Use it everywhere with no fallback
options.info: Without broad support, dropping a fallback would break the feature for many users.

options.text: Never use it under any circumstance
options.info: It can be used progressively with a fallback; “limited” is not “forbidden”.

options.text: It is the same as widely available
options.info: Limited availability is explicitly not yet Baseline; it is less supported than widely available.

questions.explanation: Limited availability means uneven support: use progressively with feature detection and a fallback.

questions.text: Order these support stages from least supported to most supported.
questions.explanation: Support grows in stages: a feature starts experimental or of limited availability, becomes Baseline newly available when it ships across the core browsers, and later Baseline widely available once it has been interoperable for a long time.

questions.text: "New" does not mean "unusable": a Baseline newly available feature can be used today, ideally with awareness of older browser versions.
questions.explanation: A common misconception is that new features must be avoided. A newly available Baseline feature is interoperable across the core browsers now; just account for users on older installed versions, with a fallback where it matters.

questions.text: "Old" does not mean "forbidden": a long-standing, widely supported element is usually the safest choice, not something to avoid.
questions.explanation: Another misconception is that older means worse. A widely available element is the most reliable; the real question is whether an element is deprecated, not merely whether it is old.

questions.text: The <center> element centres content. What is its status and modern replacement?

options.text: Deprecated/obsolete; centre with CSS (e.g. text-align or margin:auto)
options.info: <center> is an obsolete presentational element. Centring is a styling concern handled in CSS, for example text-align:center or margin-inline:auto.
<center> is obsolete; presentational elements like it were removed in favour of CSS.
It is old and obsolete, not experimental.
There is no <middle> element; centring is done with CSS.

questions.explanation: <center> is obsolete; centre with CSS. Presentation moved out of HTML long ago.

questions.text: The <font> element set text colour and size. What is its status and replacement?

options.text: Deprecated/obsolete; set colour and size with CSS
options.info: <font> is an obsolete presentational element. Use CSS properties like color and font-size instead.
<font> is obsolete; styling belongs in CSS, not in presentational elements.
<font> is old and obsolete, not a new Baseline feature.
There is no <text> element in HTML for this; use CSS.

questions.explanation: <font> is obsolete; colour and size are CSS. A classic deprecated-element example.

questions.text: The <marquee> element scrolled text across the screen. What is its status?

options.text: Deprecated/obsolete; achieve motion with CSS animations if truly needed
options.info: <marquee> is obsolete. If scrolling motion is genuinely required, use CSS animations — and consider users who prefer reduced motion.
<marquee> is obsolete, not modern or recommended.
It is a legacy, obsolete element, not experimental.
There is no <scroll> element; use CSS animation instead.

questions.explanation: <marquee> is obsolete; use CSS animation sparingly (and respect reduced-motion) instead.

questions.text: Match each deprecated element to its modern replacement.
questions.explanation: The obsolete presentational elements all map to CSS: centring, colour/size and motion are styling, which belongs in CSS, not in HTML elements.

questions.text: The <tt> element rendered teletype (monospaced) text. What should you use instead today?

options.text: A semantic element like <code>/<kbd>/<samp>, or CSS font-family for pure styling
options.info: <tt> is obsolete. Where the text is code, keyboard input or sample output, use the semantic element; where it is only a monospaced look, use CSS font-family.
<tt> is obsolete; prefer a semantic element or CSS.
There is no <monospace> element in HTML.
There is no <teletype> element in HTML.

questions.explanation: <tt> is obsolete: use a semantic element (<code>/<kbd>/<samp>) by meaning, or CSS for a monospaced look.

questions.text: The input type "datetime" was removed from the HTML standard, and datetime-local should be used instead.
questions.explanation: The global type="datetime" was removed because of implementation problems; for a local date and time use type="datetime-local" (or separate date and time inputs). Knowing what was removed is part of reading status.

questions.text: As of 2025, what is the Baseline status of the <dialog> element?

options.text: Baseline widely available — safe to use in production
options.info: <dialog> reached Baseline and is widely available across the major browsers as of 2025, so it is a safe default for dialogs.
<dialog> is no longer experimental; it is widely available.
<dialog> is current and recommended, not deprecated.
<dialog> is part of the standard and widely supported.

questions.explanation: <dialog> is Baseline widely available in 2025 — a modern element that is safe to rely on.

questions.text: As of 2025, how should you treat the <search> element's availability?

options.text: Recently Baseline; usable, with a role="search" fallback consideration for older browsers
options.info: <search> became Baseline relatively recently; it is usable now, and for very old browsers a container with role="search" was the previous pattern.

options.text: It has existed for decades and is universally supported
options.info: <search> is a recent addition, not a decades-old element.
<search> is new and recommended, not deprecated.

options.text: It is a JavaScript API, not an element
options.info: <search> is a real HTML element exposing the search landmark.

questions.explanation: <search> is a recently-Baseline element: usable now, with the old role="search" pattern as a fallback for very old browsers.

questions.text: As of 2025, what is a fair description of the Popover API (the popover attribute)?

options.text: Recently Baseline / newly available across the major browsers
options.info: The Popover API reached Baseline relatively recently and is newly/broadly available across the major browsers as of 2025; use feature detection if you must support older versions.
The Popover API is recent, not decades old.
It is new and advancing, not obsolete.
It is interoperable across the major browsers, not single-browser.

questions.explanation: The popover attribute is a recent, newly/broadly available feature in 2025 — not old, not obsolete.

questions.text: As of 2025, what is the status of the experimental <geolocation> element?

options.text: Experimental / limited availability — a proposal to watch, not for production
options.info: The <geolocation> element is experimental with limited availability as of late 2025; it is an early proposal and should not be relied on in production yet.
It is not widely available; it is experimental and barely supported so far.
It is new and experimental, not deprecated.
It is a very new proposal, not long-standing.

questions.explanation: The <geolocation> element is experimental / limited availability in 2025 — watch it, do not ship it. (Low-weight status question.)

questions.text: Which of these elements are deprecated/obsolete and should be replaced with CSS or a semantic element? Select every correct answer.

options.info: <center> is obsolete; centre with CSS.
<marquee> is obsolete; use CSS animation sparingly.
<main> is a current, recommended semantic landmark, not deprecated.
<big> is obsolete; use CSS font-size.

questions.explanation: <center>, <marquee> and <big> are obsolete presentational elements; <main> is a current semantic element.

questions.text: Deprecated elements may still render in browsers for backward compatibility, but you should not use them in new pages.
questions.explanation: Browsers keep rendering obsolete elements so old pages do not break, but they are removed from the standard and discouraged. New pages should use the modern CSS or semantic replacement.

questions.text: As of 2025, what is the Baseline status of <progress> and <meter>?

options.text: Widely available — both are long-established and safe to use
options.info: <progress> and <meter> have been interoperable for many years and are Baseline widely available, so they are safe defaults.
They are established, not experimental.
They are current and recommended.
Both remain in the standard and are widely supported.

questions.explanation: <progress> and <meter> are widely available — reliable, established elements.

questions.text: As of 2025, how available is the <selectedcontent> element (used with customizable select)?

options.text: New / limited availability — part of recent customizable-select work, not yet broadly supported
options.info: <selectedcontent> is part of recent customizable-select features with limited availability as of 2025; use it only with care and fallbacks.
It is a very recent addition, not years old.
It is new, not deprecated.
<selectedcontent> is an element, not a JS API.

questions.explanation: <selectedcontent> is new and of limited availability in 2025 — a rare/new element with little weight here.

questions.text: Order these by how long they have been dependable, from the newest/experimental to the longest-established.
questions.explanation: The experimental <geolocation> element is the newest and least supported; the popover attribute reached Baseline recently; <main> has been widely available for years. Status, not age in isolation, drives the decision.

questions.text: When deciding whether to use a feature, checking its Baseline status (and providing a fallback if it is not widely available) is more reliable than guessing from its age.
questions.explanation: Age alone is misleading: some old things are deprecated, some new things are already Baseline. Checking the current Baseline status and adding a fallback where support is limited is the dependable approach.

questions.text: The <acronym> element is obsolete. Which element replaced it?

options.info: <abbr> replaced the obsolete <acronym>; it marks both abbreviations and acronyms, with the expansion in its title attribute.
There is no <short> element in HTML.
There is no <initial> element in HTML.
There is no <acr> element; the replacement is <abbr>.

questions.explanation: The obsolete <acronym> was replaced by <abbr>, which covers both abbreviations and acronyms.

questions.text: If you add motion with CSS as a modern replacement for <marquee>, what accessibility setting should you respect?

options.text: prefers-reduced-motion, to tone down or remove animation for users who ask for less motion
options.info: The prefers-reduced-motion media query lets users request reduced animation; respecting it avoids discomfort for people sensitive to motion — something <marquee> never considered.
That is for light/dark theming, not motion.
That is about contrast levels, not motion.
prefers-reduced-motion is exactly the setting for motion.

questions.explanation: Replace <marquee> with CSS animation only while respecting prefers-reduced-motion for motion-sensitive users.
